newsitem.title: SPAIN: Peseta seen protected by Bank of Spain cushion.
newsitem.headline: Peseta seen protected by Bank of Spain cushion.

text.p: Fresh uncertainties surrounding a European single currency could signal high volatility ahead for the Spanish peseta, but the Bank of Spain can comfortably defend the currency, analysts said on Thursday .

The possibility of a Socialist victory in Sunday's French parliamentary election runoff and a dispute between the German government and the Bundesbank over revaluing gold reserves prompted a sudden drop in the peseta on Wednesday.
"The peseta will go through a situation of uncertainty until the political situation in France and Germany is clarified," said Cesar Cantalapiedra, an analyst at AFI.
Rumours that Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer would resign over the gold dispute, which were later denied, also weighed on the peseta.
In the afternoon the Bank of Spain intervened to defend the unit, with other European central banks seen supporting their own currencies.
After briefly touching 85.00 versus the mark in New York, the peseta rebounded to 84.65, a level which is seen as a platform for new mark buying.

"The peseta has come from a very stable situation and although we don't see any reason to worry, there will be more times in future when Bank of Spain intervention will be needed to prevent the peseta going above 85.00," said Antonio Villarroyo, a foreign exchange analyst at Merrill Lynch in Madrid.
He added that the Bank of Spain has ample foreign currency reserves to comfortably defend the currency.
Spain has one of the highest levels of reserves in Europe -- in the last 12 months, central bank reserves rose by 32 percent to $65.9 billion.
On the domestic front, experts agreed nothing has changed for the peseta.

"No one doubts Spain's good chances of participating in the founding group for monetary union but events in other countries have sowed doubts about a possible delay of the whole project," said Villarroya.
Cantalapiedra agreed. "The risk of a delay today is better than yesterday," he said.
Analysts said the biggest risk to the planned single currency lies in the confrontation between the Bundesbank and German government over the revaluation of gold reserves.
"The Euro project is not very well liked by public opinion in Germany, and if this gels and the German government pulls back, we face a serious risk of the project being delayed, Cantalapiedra said.
He added that if the German government imposes its revaluation of gold reserves and uses the surplus generated to reduce debt, peripheral currencies will benefit because it will clear the way to EMU.
The French election was less significant, experts said.

"Both the centre-right and the left in France are in favour of the euro it's just that in the case of a Socialist victory, the interpretation of the criteria could take a more flexible form," said one trader. That would benefit peripheral currencies like the peseta, he added.
In currency markets, where the monetary turmoil between 1992 and 1995 that led to devaluation of the peseta has not been forgotten, Wednesday's slide did not cause panic.
However Villarroyo concluded that there was not much danger to peseta stability, but from now onwards it would perhaps be more difficult to earn from Spanish assets.
"Yesterday's events show that we have to be more alert to news moving the market, and, above all, to any news that throw into doubt the start of EMU in 1999," he said.
